explanation.text: Where can the Riemann zeta function vanish? Its known zeros at $-2,-4,-6,\ldots$ are called trivial zeros. The point $s=1$ is a pole, where the meromorphic function blows up. The Riemann Hypothesis puts every other zero on the vertical line $\operatorname{Re}s=1/2$. The location matters for counting primes. In the smoothed count used in the paper, a zero $\rho$ contributes a term proportional to $x^\rho$. A zero farther to the right has a larger real part and gives a faster-growing term. Alpöge’s proof rules out zeros to the right of the line for all Dirichlet $L$-functions, including $\zeta$ at modulus one. The zeta functional equation rules out a remaining zero to the left by reflecting it to $1-s$.
